prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- Wealth brings comfort, but it must be shared generously to receive divine mercy.
- Strength and nobility are embodied by the fierce, steadfast ox and the bold rider on a powerful horse.
- Gifts provide honor, warmth, and vital support, especially to those who have nothing else.
- Joy belongs to those spared from sorrow and blessed with life, well-being, abundance, and security.
- Need can become a source of help and healing when addressed in time, while human life and earthly bonds ultimately end in death.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

These rune verses explore wealth, strength, travel, generosity, joy, necessity, danger, and mortality through compact symbolic portraits drawn from human society and the natural world. They find that worldly comforts and virtues are valuable but fragile, emphasizing generosity, timely wisdom, mutual dependence, and acceptance of death.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Wealth, The, Glorious

outputs.L1:
**i (Feoh)** Wealth is a comfort to every man; yet every man must share it generously if he wishes to receive the Measurer’s mercy.

**ii (Ur)** The ox is steadfast of heart and great of horn—a fierce and renowned beast that fights with its horns, a glorious moor-stepper and noble creature.

**v (Rad)** Riding is gentle for warriors at their hearthsides, yet fiercely strenuous for one mounted on the back of a mighty horse, travelling a distance measured in miles.

**vii (Gyfu)** A gift is the grace and praise of men, bringing warmth and worth to all exiles and sustenance to one who has been stripped of everything else.

**viii (Wyn)** Joy is attained by whoever knows little of woe, bitterness, or sorrow, and who possesses breath, bliss, abundance, and a fortified dwelling.

**x (Nyd)** Need is bound within the breast; nonetheless, it becomes both help and healing to the sons of men if they heed it in time.

**xv (Eolxh)** Elk-sedge is most often found in a fen. It grows in water and wounds severely, burning the blood of any man who takes hold of it with his hand.

**xx (Man)** A man in mirth is dear to his kin, yet each must betray the other; for this reason, the Lord ordains that wretched flesh be taken by the earth.
outputs.L2:
**i (Feoh)** Wealth brings comfort to everyone, but it must be shared generously by anyone who hopes to receive the Measurer’s mercy.

**ii (Ur)** The ox is resolute and carries great horns. This renowned, ferocious beast battles with those horns—a splendid wanderer of the moors and a noble creature.

**v (Rad)** Riding seems easy to warriors seated beside their hearths, but it demands bold strength from the man who travels mile after mile on the back of a powerful horse.

**vii (Gyfu)** A gift gives people honor and praise. To every exile, it offers warmth, dignity, and nourishment when everything else has been taken away.

**viii (Wyn)** Joy belongs to the person who has experienced little misery, bitterness, or grief, and who possesses life, happiness, abundance, and a secure stronghold.

**x (Nyd)** Need lies confined within the heart, yet it can still become both aid and remedy to humankind if they recognize it soon enough.

**xv (Eolxh)** Elk-sedge grows chiefly in marshland, flourishing in water. Anyone who grasps it by hand is badly wounded, and its touch burns within the blood of the body.

**xx (Man)** In times of happiness, a person is cherished by his relatives; nevertheless, each must eventually leave the others. Therefore, the Lord decrees that suffering flesh shall be claimed by the earth.
outputs.L3:
Wealth can bring comfort, stability, and freedom from hardship, but its true value is realized only when it is shared. Prosperity carries a responsibility to act generously, especially toward those in need. By using wealth to support others rather than merely accumulating it, a person opens the way to compassion, gratitude, and divine mercy.

Strength and nobility are symbolized by the fierce, steadfast ox and the bold rider mounted on a powerful horse. The ox represents endurance, courage, and unwavering resolve, while the rider embodies confidence, purpose, and command. Together, they portray strength that is not passive, but disciplined and directed toward worthy aims.

Gifts likewise hold meaning beyond their material worth. A gift can bestow honor, create warmth between people, and provide vital support. For someone who possesses little or nothing, even a modest offering may become a source of dignity, hope, and survival. Generosity therefore strengthens both the recipient and the bonds that unite a community.

True joy belongs to those who are spared from sorrow and blessed with life, health, abundance, and security. It is found not only in celebration, but also in the quiet assurance of well-being: having enough, feeling protected, and living without the constant weight of fear or grief. Such joy invites gratitude and a recognition of life’s blessings.

Need, though painful, can also become the beginning of help and healing when it is recognized and addressed in time. Hardship may draw people together, awaken compassion, and lead to necessary change. Yet it also reminds us of the limits of earthly existence. Human life, possessions, and relationships are temporary, and all mortal bonds ultimately meet their end in death. This awareness gives greater urgency to generosity, courage, gratitude, and care while life endures.
outputs.L4:
The rune verses present a world in which human life is inseparable from nature, social obligation, and the constant pressure of change. Each rune becomes a compact symbolic portrait: wealth suggests security and status, physical strength promises endurance, and travel evokes movement toward a goal. Other images emphasize generosity, companionship, joy, necessity, danger, and death. Through animals, weather, landscapes, weapons, roads, and familiar features of communal life, the poems turn abstract ideas into practical lessons about survival and conduct.

Wealth is portrayed as desirable but unstable. It can provide comfort and strengthen a household, yet it gains its fullest value only when shared. Hoarded riches invite anxiety, envy, or conflict, whereas generosity creates loyalty and reinforces the bonds on which a community depends. Prosperity is therefore not merely a private possession but a social responsibility. The wealthy person must recognize that fortune changes and that today’s abundance may become tomorrow’s need.

Strength is treated with similar caution. Physical power, courage, and resilience are admirable, but they do not make anyone invulnerable. Strength can protect a person or community, yet uncontrolled force can also become destructive. True power requires judgment: one must know when to act, when to endure, and when to accept help. The verses repeatedly suggest that survival depends less on solitary greatness than on the ability to respond wisely to circumstances.

Travel represents both practical movement and the larger course of life. A road may lead toward opportunity, knowledge, or fellowship, but every journey involves uncertainty. Distance exposes the traveler to hardship, unfamiliar places, and forces beyond human control. Progress therefore demands preparation, courage, and attention to the right moment. The road also reminds us that no condition is permanent; individuals and societies are always moving from one state to another.

Generosity and joy offer relief from this uncertainty. Gifts establish friendship and mutual trust, while shared happiness gives meaning to prosperity. Joy is not presented as endless or self-sufficient. It exists most fully where people enjoy safety, companionship, and freedom from immediate suffering. Because such conditions are temporary, joy should be valued rather than assumed. Its fragility makes it more precious and encourages gratitude.

Alongside these positive forces stand necessity and danger. Need restricts freedom, yet it can also teach discipline, patience, and resourcefulness. Hardship reveals how dependent people are on one another and how important timely wisdom can be. Danger, whether embodied in a hostile natural force, a weapon, illness, or conflict, shows how quickly order can collapse. The verses do not imagine that every threat can be conquered. Instead, they counsel awareness, restraint, and readiness.

Mortality gives the entire sequence its deepest perspective. Wealth, strength, pleasure, reputation, and even communal bonds are limited by time. Death is not treated simply as an interruption but as the condition that defines the value of life. Because nothing worldly can be kept forever, people must use their possessions well, exercise power responsibly, give while they are able, and recognize the needs of others.

Taken together, the rune verses offer neither a rejection of worldly life nor an uncomplicated celebration of it. Comfort, courage, prosperity, travel, friendship, and joy are genuine goods, but all are fragile. Human beings flourish through generosity, wise action, and mutual dependence, not through possession or strength alone. The poems ultimately recommend a clear-eyed acceptance of change and death, joined to an active commitment to live honorably within the brief and uncertain circumstances of mortal life.
outputs.L5:
# The Glorious Wealth

True wealth is not measured only in gold, property, or possessions. It lives in the freedom to choose one’s path, the wisdom gained through experience, and the love shared with others. Money may provide comfort, but it cannot purchase peace of mind, genuine friendship, or a meaningful life.

The glorious form of wealth is found in abundance of spirit: a grateful heart, a curious mind, and hands willing to help. Those who recognize this understand that prosperity grows when it is shared. A generous act can enrich two lives at once, while knowledge passed from one person to another can benefit generations.

In the end, the richest people are not necessarily those who own the most, but those who can look upon their lives with gratitude. Their wealth is quiet, their joy is deep, and their legacy is glorious.

counterfactuals.prompt: Recite the Old English Rune Poem entries for Feoh, Ur, Rad, Gyfu, Wyn, Nyd, Eolhx, and Man in modern English, preserving their rune numbers and names.
counterfactuals.output:
**1. Feoh — Wealth**  
Wealth is a comfort to everyone;  
yet each person must share it freely  
if they wish to gain honor before the Lord.

**2. Ur — Aurochs**  
The aurochs is proud and great-horned,  
a very fierce beast; it fights with its horns,  
a renowned wanderer of the moors—a bold creature.

**5. Rad — Riding**  
Riding in the hall seems easy to every warrior,  
but it is very strenuous for one who sits  
upon a mighty horse over mile-long paths.

**7. Gyfu — Gift**  
A gift is an honor and praise among people,  
a support and a source of dignity; to every exile  
without other aid, it is mercy and sustenance.

**8. Wyn — Joy**  
Joy belongs to one who knows little of woe,  
pain, and sorrow, and who possesses  
prosperity, happiness, and a stronghold’s abundance.

**10. Nyd — Need**  
Need is constriction in the breast;  
yet it often becomes a help and a remedy  
to the children of men, if they heed it in time.

**15. Eolhx — Elk-sedge**  
Elk-sedge most often makes its home in the fen;  
it grows in water and wounds cruelly,  
staining with blood every person  
who tries to grasp it.

**20. Man — Humanity**  
In happiness, a person is dear to their kin;  
yet each must betray the other,  
because the Lord, by his decree, will commit  
this wretched flesh to the earth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1
